TLSNotary v0.1.0-alpha.15, MPC-TLS, TLS 1.2. ### Two-agent payment demo 1 paid · 4 refused Agent A quotes the USD→EUR rate from api.frankfurter.dev (ECB reference rates). Agent B pays a €10,000 invoice in dollars at that rate. Every message between them passes through a relay that tries to cheat. Agent B acts only on a value inside a valid receipt, from the right server, for the right request, less than ten minutes old. Round | The relay | Agent B --- | --- | --- 1 | Forwards the message unchanged | Computes the payment at the witnessed rate 2 | Changes the rate, leaves the receipt | Refuses: the claim does not match the receipt 3 | Changes the rate and edits the receipt to match | Refuses: the receipt fails verification 4 | Swaps in a genuine receipt for USD→GBP | Refuses: the receipt answers a different request 5 | Strips the receipt | Refuses: unwitnessed claim The agents are scripted MCP clients, not language models, so runs repeat exactly. No money moved; agent B computes the payment. ~10 ms to verify a receipt, offline 2.8–4.0 s per witnessed call, MPC mode 27× less traffic in proxy mode 0 software installed on the server Measured on one machine with the witness running locally. A remote witness has not been measured yet. Limits ## What a receipt does not prove. A receipt proves what a named server sent, and when. Read it as exactly that. It does not prove * That the server told the truth. A receipt shows what api.weather.gov said, not the weather. * Anything about a server the operator controls. That receipt is still the operator’s word, now fixed in time and bytes. * That the agent sent every action through the witness. That takes credential custody or egress control. * Independence, when one party runs both the agent side and the witness. High-value receipts should carry more than one witness. * That the content is safe to act on. A genuine page can still carry a prompt injection. Engine limits today: TLS 1.2 only (TLS 1.3 is on TLSNotary’s roadmap), pre-release software, and no compressed or streamed responses. ## Two tools your agent already knows how to call. Histor ships as a CLI and an MCP server, so it works in Claude Code, Cursor and any MCP client. Receipts are content-addressed: agents pass a short receipt_id instead of 15 KB of base64. witnessed_fetch(url, fields?, mode?) GETs an https:// URL through a Histor witness. Returns the server, time, request and disclosed fields, plus a receipt_id. verify_receipt(receipt_id | receipt, expect_server?) Checks a receipt another agent handed you, offline. Returns what it proves, or the reason it fails. witnessed_request(url, method, body, request_fields?) POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE. Credentials for the target live on the server, so the model never sees a secret. The request body is committed and stays hidden unless you disclose named fields. Your AI client trusts the tool descriptions an MCP server sends it — and a server can change them after you approved it. HISTOR keeps a public, signed record of what every remote MCP server in the official registry advertised, and tells you the day it changed. Remote endpoints: it lists tools and never calls one. Registry packages: bounded canary calls run inside the isolated sandbox. It never says a server is safe — it tells you what was said, and when. What HISTOR is for ## Tool descriptions are instructions. They should not change behind your back. The problem ### A server can change what your model reads When you connect an MCP server, its tool descriptions go straight to the model as instructions. A server can pass your review with harmless descriptions and change them next week — one added sentence is all a prompt injection needs, and most clients never ask you again. What HISTOR does ### It keeps the public record Every day HISTOR reads what each remote (streamable-HTTP) endpoint in the official MCP registry advertises, fingerprints it, signs what it saw and appends it to a log that can only grow. When a server's definitions change, the change gets a date and a diff. What you get ### A second pair of eyes you can check Look up any server before you trust it. Paste what your client received and learn whether everyone else sees the same thing. Follow changes in a feed, or put a badge in your README. Every answer is signed, so you can verify it instead of believing it. ### Who it is for People who use MCP servers in Claude, Cursor or any client — check a server before you connect it, and again when it changes. Agent builders whose agents connect to servers on their own — call /check before trusting a tool set. Registries and directories that want more than stars and download counts — show when a listing's tools last changed. Server authors who want to show a stable, documented history — add the badge, and every change you ship is dated in public. ### Four words used on this page Tool definitions The name, description and input schema of each tool a server offers — the text your model reads. Pinned HISTOR has recorded a fingerprint (digest) of the exact definitions it saw, so any later change is detectable. Label One signed statement about one observation: what was seen, what matched, whether it changed. Anyone can verify it offline. Signed tree head The log's signed summary after each crawl. Comparing two of them proves nothing was deleted or rewritten in between. ### Limits 512 MB of memory, one CPU, 64 MB of /tmp. 360 s to install, 150 s to start and answer; up to 15 tools called once each with canary arguments, 8 s per call. ### Configuration Only names: required variables its registry entry declares or that it printed when it exited, and a start argument such as serve when its usage text offers one. Never a value from anyone else. ## What a label does not say The profile HISTOR implements forbids the words safe, secure, audited, certified, approved and trusted. Here is why, in the terms of what the log can and cannot show. ### Not a safety rating A pattern match is a reason to read a definition, not a finding. Three of the four methods can never return fail. There is no score to rank by, because no score HISTOR could compute would mean what a reader takes it to mean. ### Not the code Labels are about advertised text. A remote endpoint's source is never read and its tools are never invoked; a package runs only in the sandbox, against nothing real. A server can keep identical definitions and behave differently for real users; the log cannot see that, and says so inside every label. ### A change is not an accusation A version bump changes definitions too. A change is shown as a date and a diff, in amber, never red. What you do with it is yours: re-read, re-approve, or pin the old digest. ### A package as run here, not on your machine An npm or PyPI server is observed under the test conditions above: Linux, no internet, placeholder keys. One that needs Windows, a real account or the network may show fewer tools or none; its page says why it exited. ### One operator, one key Today one party runs the log. A second observer on another network is the next step, and any AIMarket hub can run one. Until then, what the key proves is who said it — not that it is true. ### Behind a login, unseen Endpoints that require authentication answer 401 to everyone without a key, including HISTOR.
